title: EDUCATION | 5.24.26 Manufactured Difficulty
author: TextSavvy
summary: TextSavvy mounts a pointed critique of education's received wisdom that students must encounter 'challenge' to truly learn. The author notes that challenge does not appear in any scientific learning model as a necessary ingredient -- it appears in ancient narrative story structures (rags to riches, man against the world) that require struggle before triumph. The educational obsession with manufactured difficulty may be borrowed from these narrative archetypes -- or from reality TV's discovery that audiences rubberneck trauma -- rather than from any empirical finding about learning. A critical distinction is drawn between genuine curricular challenge (exposure to more advanced material) and invented psychological hardship introduced for its own sake. The author argues that acquiring the knowledge we transmit to students is challenge enough; inventing additional difficulties serves administrators' records and photo galleries more than students' learning. The piece functions as a challenge to the challenge-fetish itself: what is the actual evidence that manufactured difficulty improves outcomes, and who benefits from framing education as an obstacle course?
points: * Challenge does not appear as a necessary component in any scientific model of learning -- its prominence in educational discourse may owe more to ancient narrative archetypes (rags to riches, struggle before triumph) than to empirical evidence. * The reality TV parallel is instructive: television executives discovered audiences respond to trauma stories, so trauma became ubiquitous -- educational culture may have similarly discovered that 'challenge' is a compelling narrative regardless of its learning value. * A critical distinction separates genuine curricular difficulty (material that is appropriately advanced in the instructional sequence) from manufactured psychological hardship deliberately introduced around learning. * Some challenges are certainly reliable goods -- but others may be 'mean or sadistic,' given rhetorical cover by the ad astra per aspera ('through hardship to the stars') narrative educators tell themselves. * Acquiring the knowledge we intend to transmit is itself sufficient challenge; inventing additional difficulties raises the question of whose interests are actually being served -- students', or administrators' documentation needs.
quotes: Why must 'challenge' -- nebulous, polyseminal, functionally decoupled 'challenge' -- be deliberately inserted into everyone's educational formation somewhere, somehow?

'Challenge' is not a necessary component of any scientific learning model out there. It might make for a good story, and even one that we have a hard time not writing, but this is not persuasive as an argument for the necessity of 'challenge' in learning.
Of course, students should not be protected from all challenge. But it seems to me to be challenge enough to acquire the knowledge we transmit to students. Why must we invent more challenges?
Some challenges are certainly reliable goods, whereas others may just be mean or sadistic, and only given cover by the universal story of ad astra per aspera that we tell ourselves in various ways.
Is it for the students or for our photo galleries and administrative records?
